message.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
<jats:p>In some of the earliest Buddhist literature found in Myanmar, a type of translation in which each Pali word is followed by its relevant annotative interpretation, known as <jats:italic>nissaya</jats:italic>, can be found. Previous studies (Tin Lwin 1961; Pruitt 1992; McDaniel 2008; Clark 2015) only examined what a <jats:italic>nissaya</jats:italic> is and to what literary genre <jats:italic>nissaya</jats:italic> literature belongs. In this paper, I will explore the various ways in which Burmese <jats:italic>nissaya</jats:italic> literature evolved into a mainstream monastic learning method, its role in the monastic education in Burma in particular, and further investigate whether the <jats:italic>nissayas</jats:italic> can be applied more generally and what the relationship is between <jats:italic>nissaya</jats:italic> and official Burmese Tipitaka translation. Lastly, this study argues that the Burmese <jats:italic>nissaya</jats:italic> literature can be compared to be on par with the encyclopaedic compilation on a specific subject.</jats:p>
title: Burmese Nissaya Literature: A Mainstream Monastic Education Learning Method and its Salient Features
